questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Power Rule to Compute a Limit Given a Graph
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/a086a1f616aee596a021ee4ef6bdc8723309cf8959719e9f55d6f20b845bd760.png)

If the figure above shows the graph of the function $f(x),$ then

${lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3)^{2}(5-f(x))^{3}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
From the graph we get that ${lim}_{x\to -2}f(x)=4.$ 

From the product rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3)^{2}(5-f(x))^{3}={lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3)^{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -2}(5-f(x))^{3}.
$$

We calculate the limits of each factor, separately.

Applying the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3)^{2} & ={({lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3))}^{2} \\  & ={((-2)^{2}+3)}^{2} \\  & ={(4+3)}^{2} \\  & ={7}^{2} \\  & =49\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}(5-f(x))^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to -2}(5-f(x)))}^{3} \\  & ={(5-4)}^{3} \\  & ={1}^{3} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -2}({x}^{2}+3)^{2}(5-f(x))^{3} & =49\cdot 1 \\  & =49.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Terms of a Fibonacci Sequence Given in Function Notation
questions.problem:
The recursive formula for the Fibonacci numbers is 

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n),\,f(1)=f(2)=1,\,n\ge 1.
$$

The $6$th term of the sequence is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The recursion relation is

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n).
$$

Substituting $n=1$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1+2) & =f(1+1)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =f(2)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =1+1 \\ f(3) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, substituting $n=2,3,4$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4) & =f(2+2)=f(2+1)+f(2)=f(3)+f(2)=2+1=3 \\ f(5) & =f(3+2)=f(3+1)+f(3)=f(4)+f(3)=3+2=5 \\ f(6) & =f(4+2)=f(4+1)+f(4)=f(5)+f(4)=5+3=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $6$th term of the sequence is $8.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Multiplicity of a Root of a Cubic Polynomial Using Synthetic Division
questions.problem: The multiplicity of the root $x=-5$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-15x-100$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=-5$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x+5)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x+5)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x+5)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+5)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-5$ | $1$ | $6$ | $-15$ | $-100$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-5$ | $-5$ | $100$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ | $-20$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x+5}={x}^{2}+x-20,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x+5)({x}^{2}+x-20).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x+5)(x-4)(x+5) \\  & =(x-4)(x+5)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x+5)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-5$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.knowledge_point: The Vertical Asymptote of a Transformed Logarithmic Function
questions.problem:
Find the equation of the vertical asymptote of the function $f(x)=-{log}_{2}(9-3x)+4.$

$x =$: {{x}}
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of the vertical asymptote of the function $y={log}_{2}x$ is $x=0.$

To find the equation of the vertical asymptote of $f(x),$ we set the argument of the logarithmic term equal to zero, and solve for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}9-3x & =0 \\ -3x & =-9 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the vertical asymptote is $x=3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Rule of Product
questions.problem:
Rio's Pizza offers a mix and match pizza on its menu. There are $4$ different meat types to choose from, $5$ different vegetables, $4$ different types of cheese, and $2$ different types of crust. How many different types of pizza can be made by choosing a type of meat, a vegetable, cheese and a crust?

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
Using the **rule of product**, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Number of pizzas} & =\text{Number of type of meats} \\  & \times \text{Number of type of vegetables} \\  & \times \text{Number of type of cheese} \\  & \times \text{Number of type of crust} \\  & =4\times 5\times 4\times 2 \\  & =160.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $160$ types of pizza can be made with the given ingredients.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Multiplicity of a Root of a Cubic Polynomial Using Grouping
questions.worked_solution:
We factor the cubic by grouping, and simplify until the polynomial is fully factored:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =2{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+32x+16 \\  & ={x}^{2}(2x+1)+16(2x+1) \\  & =({x}^{2}+16)(2x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the factor $({x}^{2}+16)$ cannot be factored any further, and it does not have any real roots.

The only real root of $p(x)$ comes from the factor $(2x+1).$ This factor has a root of $x=-\frac{1}{2},$ and the exponent of the factor is $1.$ Therefore, the root $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, there is no root with multiplicity $2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Multiplicity of a Root of a Cubic Polynomial Using the GCF
questions.problem:
Which root(s) of the polynomial $p(x)=5{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2}$ have multiplicity $2?$

$x =$: {{x}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. 

For this polynomial, we can factor by noting that the greatest common factor of $5{x}^{3}$ and $-15{x}^{2}$ is $5{x}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =5{x}^{3}-15{x}^{2} \\  & =5{x}^{2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

To find the roots and their multiplicities, we look at the factors:

- The factor $x$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

- The factor $(x-3)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=3$ has multiplicity $1.$

In conclusion, only the root $x=0$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Multiplicity of a Root of a Cubic Polynomial Using Synthetic Division
questions.problem: The multiplicity of the root $x=1$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}+4{x}^{2}-11x+6$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=1$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-1)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $4$ | $-11$ | $6$ |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $5$ | $-6$ |
|  | $1$ | $5$ | $-6$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-1}={x}^{2}+5x-6,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x-1)({x}^{2}+5x-6).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-1)(x-1)(x+6) \\  & =(x+6)(x-1)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-1)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=1$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.worked_solution:

$$
f(n+2)=f(n+1)+f(n).
$$

Substituting $n=1$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1+2) & =f(1+1)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =f(2)+f(1) \\ f(3) & =5+0 \\ f(3) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $n=2$ into the recursive formula gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2+2) & =f(2+1)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =f(3)+f(2) \\ f(4) & =5+5 \\ f(4) & =10\end{aligned}
$$

We continue this process to compute $f(5)$ and $f(6)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(5) & =f(3+2)=f(3+1)+f(3)=f(4)+f(3)=10+5=15 \\ f(6) & =f(4+2)=f(4+1)+f(4)=f(5)+f(4)=15+10=25\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(6)=25.$

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-2$ | $1$ | $8$ | $20$ | $16$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-2$ | $-12$ | $-16$ |
|  | $1$ | $6$ | $8$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x+2}={x}^{2}+6x+8,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x+2)({x}^{2}+6x+8).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x+2)(x+2)(x+4) \\  & =(x+4)(x+2)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x+2)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=-2$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Rule of Product
questions.problem:
How many possible outcomes are there if a coin is flipped twice, a six-sided die is rolled three times, and a tetrahedral (four-sided) die is rolled once?

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
For the coin, there are $2$ outcomes: "Heads" and "Tails".

For the six-sided die, there is a total of $6$ outcomes: $1,2,3,4,5,6.$

For the tetrahedral die, there is a total of $4$ outcomes: $1,2,3,4.$

Using the **rule of product**, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total Possible Outcomes} & =\text{Number of outcomes when the coin is flipped the first time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the coin is flipped the second time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the first time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the second time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the six-sided die is rolled the third time} \\  & \times \text{Number of outcomes when the tetrahedral die is rolled the one time} \\  & =2\times 2\times 6\times 6\times 6\times 4 \\  & ={2}^{2}\times {6}^{3}\times 4 \\  & =4\times 216\times 4 \\  & =3\,456.\end{aligned}
$$

So, there are $3\,456$ possible outcomes.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Argument of a Complex Number in the Second Quadrant
questions.problem:
Find, **in radians**, the argument of $z=-4+6\text{i}.$ Round your final answer to **two decimal places**.

**Hint**: The argument of a complex number is in the range $[0,2\pi ).$ 

$\operatorname{arg}(z)\approx $
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Let's plot $z$ in the complex plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/325444dbc509efd27f6c5bf16c751b137532e2566a9dfaa69f92d9ce16bac51b.png)

The complex number $z$ lies in the second quadrant of the complex plane. Hence $\frac{\pi }{2}<\operatorname{arg}(z)<\pi .$ 

If $\alpha $ is the angle that $z$ makes with the negative real axis, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}\alpha  & =\frac{6}{4} \\ \alpha  & =\operatorname{arctan}(\frac{6}{4}) \\  & =0.982\text{ }793…\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arg}(z)=\pi -0.982\text{ }793…\approx 2.16,
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Possible Roots of a Polynomial Using the Rational Roots Theorem
questions.problem:
According to the rational roots theorem, What could be a root of the polynomial $f(x)=4{x}^{7}-12{x}^{4}+5{x}^{2}-3x+10?$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $10,$ and the leading coefficient is $4.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }10}{\text{factor of }4}.
$$

Of the given answer choices, only $\frac{5}{4}$ takes the above form since the numerator $(5)$ is a factor of $10$ and the denominator $(4)$ is a factor of $4.$

questions.problem: According to the rational root theorem, the polynomial $f(x)=25{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}-x-5$ has{{field-1}} *potential* rational roots.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial:

- The constant term is $-5,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 5.$

- The leading coefficient is $25,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$, $\pm 5$, and $\pm 25.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1},\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{5},\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{25}, \\ \pm \frac{5}{1},\text{ }\pm \frac{5}{5},\text{ }\pm \frac{5}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we reduce the fractions to their lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1,\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{5},\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{25}, \\ \pm 5,\text{ }\pm 1,\text{ }\pm \frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that some potential roots are duplicates (shown above in red). Removing these duplicates and listing those remaining in order from least to greatest in absolute value, we have

$$
\pm \frac{1}{25},\,\pm \frac{1}{5},\,\pm 1,\,\pm 5.
$$

This makes a total of $8$ potential roots. (Remember that each $\pm $ sign accounts for $2$ roots, and $2\cdot 4=8.$)

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.

- The constant term is $12,$ and its factors are $\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6$ and $\pm 12.$

- The leading coefficient is $5,$ and its factors are $\pm 1$ and $\pm 5.$

First, we list out all the possibilities for the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm \frac{1}{1}, & \pm \frac{1}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{2}{1}, & \pm \frac{2}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{3}{1}, & \pm \frac{3}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{4}{1}, & \pm \frac{4}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{6}{1}, & \pm \frac{6}{5}, \\ \pm \frac{12}{1}, & \pm \frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}

Next, we reduce the fractions to lowest terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\pm 1, & \pm \frac{1}{5}, \\ \pm 2, & \pm \frac{2}{5}, \\ \pm 3, & \pm \frac{3}{5}, \\ \pm 4, & \pm \frac{4}{5}, \\ \pm 6, & \pm \frac{6}{5}, \\ \pm 12, & \pm \frac{12}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

questions.problem: Given that the polynomial $f(x)=27{x}^{3}-54{x}^{2}+36x-8$ has a root in the interval $(\frac{1}{2},1),$ the sum of the **distinct** real roots of $f(x)$ equals{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-8$ and the leading coefficient is $27.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-8}{\text{factor of }27}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \pm \frac{1}{27},\,\pm \frac{2}{27},\,\pm \frac{1}{9},\,\pm \frac{4}{27},\,\pm \frac{2}{9},\,\frac{8}{27},\,\pm \frac{1}{3},\,\pm \frac{4}{9}, \\  & \pm \frac{2}{3},\,\pm \frac{8}{9},\,\pm 1,\,\pm \frac{4}{3},\,\pm 2,\,\pm \frac{8}{3},\,\pm 4,\,\pm 8\end{aligned}
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(\frac{1}{2},1)$ are $\frac{2}{3}$ and $\frac{8}{9}.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-\frac{2}{3})$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\frac{2}{3}$ | $27$ | $-54$ | $36$ | $-8$ |
|  | $↓$ | $18$ | $-24$ | $8$ |
|  | $27$ | $-36$ | $12$ | $0$ |

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-\frac{2}{3})(27{x}^{2}-36x+12).\end{aligned}
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-\frac{2}{3})(27{x}^{2}-36x+12) \\  & =3(x-\frac{2}{3})(9{x}^{2}-12x+4) \\  & =3(x-\frac{2}{3})(3x-2)^{2} \\  & =(3x-2)(3x-2)^{2} \\  & =(3x-2)^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the only root of $f(x)$ is $x=\frac{2}{3}.$

questions.problem:
Given that the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-10x+8$ has one of its roots in the interval $(-5,-1),$ find the sum of the distinct real roots of $f(x).$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $8$ and the leading coefficient is $1.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }8}{\text{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 4,\pm 8
$$

Of these roots, the only roots in the interval $(-5,-1),$ are $-4$ and $-2.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x+4)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-4$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-10$ | $8$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-4$ | $12$ | $-8$ |
|  | $1$ | $-3$ | $2$ | $0$ |

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x+4)({x}^{2}-3x+2) \\  & =(x+4)(x-1)(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find the roots $x=-4,1,2.$ Summing these roots, we get

$$
-4+1+2=-1.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, the rational roots theorem states that any rational roots of the polynomial must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of the constant term}}{\text{factor of the leading coefficient}}.
$$

For the given polynomial $f(x),$ the constant term is $-24$ and the leading coefficient is $1.$ So, any rational roots of $f(x)$ must take the form

$$
\pm \frac{\text{factor of }-24}{\text{factor of }1}.
$$

Therefore, the possible rational roots are as follows:

$$
\pm 1,\,\pm 2,\,\pm 3,\,\pm 4,\,\pm 6,\,\pm 8,\,\pm 12,\,\pm 24.
$$

Of these roots, the only root in the interval $(2,4)$ is $3.$

Now, let's use synthetic division to test whether $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x).$ We get the following:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $3$ | $1$ | $3$ | $-10$ | $-24$ |
|  | $↓$ | $3$ | $18$ | $24$ |
|  | $1$ | $6$ | $8$ | $0$ |

Since the remainder is $0,$ we conclude that $(x-3)$ is indeed a factor of $f(x).$ Moreover, we have

$$
f(x)=(x-3)({x}^{2}+6x+8).
$$

Since the highest-degree factor is now a quadratic, we can continue factoring using the usual methods:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =(x-3)({x}^{2}+6x+8) \\  & =(x-3)(x+2)(x+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the factors equal to $0,$ we find that, in ascending order, the roots of the polynomial are $x=-4,$ $x=-2,$ and $x=3.$

questions.problem:
Consider the quadratic equation

$$
7{x}^{2}-9x+2=0.
$$

**Without** solving the equation, determine the sum of its solutions.

questions.worked_solution:
Suppose the quadratic equation

$$
a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0
$$

has the solutions $x={x}_{1}$ and $x={x}_{2},$ where $a\ne 0.$ 

Then, Vieta's formulas state the following:

- The sum of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-\frac{b}{a}.
$$

- The product of the solutions is given by

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{c}{a}.
$$

For the given quadratic equation, we have

$$
a=7,\,b=-9,\,c=2.
$$

Therefore, the sum of the solutions is

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{b}{a} & =-\frac{(-9)}{7}=\frac{9}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a System of Linear Equations Using Substitution
questions.worked_solution:
We have the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}b=240-20a \\ 30b+900a=6\,000\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. 

Notice that the first equation is already solved for $b:$

$$
b=240-20a
$$

So, we replace $b$ in the second equation and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}30b+900a & =6\,000 \\ 30(240-20a)+900a & =6\,000 \\ 7\,200-600a+900a & =6\,000 \\ 7\,200+300a & =6\,000 \\ 300a & =-1\,200 \\ a & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $a=-4$ into $b=240-20a,$ we can then find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}b & =240-20(-4) \\ b & =320\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-4,\,b=320.$

questions.knowledge_point: Factoring Trinomials With Positive Coefficients
questions.problem:
Find the minimum number of cakes the bakery needs to produce per week to make a weekly profit of $$6\,000.$

The bakery needs to produce$\,$
{{field-1}}$\,$ cakes per week.
questions.worked_solution:
From part 5, the required number of cakes $x$ is the solution to the equation

$$
4\cdot ({x}^{2}-80x+1\,500)=0.
$$

Dividing this equation by $4,$ we have

$$
{x}^{2}-80x+1\,500=0.
$$

To solve this equation, we want to find a factor pair of the constant term $(1\,500)$ that also adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-80).$ The required factors are $(-30)$ and $(-50).$

Using this factor pair, we write the linear term as $-80x=-30x-50x,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-80x+1\,500 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-30x-50x+1\,500 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-30x-50x+1\,500 & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-30x)+(-50x+1\,500) & =0 \\ x(x-30)-50(x-30) & =0 \\ (x-30)(x-50)\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the solutions are $x=30$ or $x=50.$ Since we require the minimum solution, we conclude that the bakery needs to produce $30$ cakes per week to make a profit of $$6\,000.$

questions.worked_solution:
To compute ${a}_{4},$ we first need to compute ${a}_{3}.$ So, we substitute $n=1$ into the recursive formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{1+2} & ={a}_{1+1}+{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{3} & ={a}_{2}+{a}_{1} \\ {a}_{3} & =0+(-2) \\ {a}_{3} & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to compute ${a}_{4},$ we substitute $n=2$ into the recursive formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2+2} & ={a}_{2+1}+{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{4} & ={a}_{3}+{a}_{2} \\ {a}_{4} & =-2+0 \\ {a}_{4} & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The function $f(x)=\frac{k}{3x+5}$ has an inverse function given by ${f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{2-5x}{3x}.$ What is the value of $k?$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=\frac{k}{3x+5}
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=\frac{k}{3y+5}.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{k}{3y+5} \\ x(3y+5) & =k \\ 3xy+5x & =k \\ 3xy & =k-5x \\ y & =\frac{k-5x}{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{k-5x}{3x}.
$$

Comparing our answer with the given expression, we conclude that $k=2.$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}({0}^{∘})=1.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}({0}^{∘})=0.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{tan}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}({0}^{∘})=\frac{\operatorname{sin}({0}^{∘})}{\operatorname{cos}({0}^{∘})}=\frac{0}{1}=0.
$$

Now, let's consider the angle ${270}^{∘}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle ${270}^{∘}$ corresponds to the point $(0,-1).$

- Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}({270}^{∘})=0.$

- Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}({270}^{∘})=-1.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{cot}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cot}({270}^{∘})=\frac{\operatorname{cos}({270}^{∘})}{\operatorname{sin}({270}^{∘})}=\frac{0}{-1}=0.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{tan}({0}^{∘})+\operatorname{cot}({270}^{∘})=0+0=0.
$$

First, we write the equation in standard form by bringing all of the terms to the left-hand side. This gives the equation

We can find the roots of a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula:

$$
x=\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}

$$

$$

Therefore, the equation has two solutions, $x=-10+4\,\text{i}$ and $x=-10-4\,\text{i}.$

questions.problem: The multiplicity of the root $x=1$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}-7{x}^{2}+14x-8$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=1$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-1)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-1)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-1)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $1$ | $-7$ | $14$ | $-8$ |
|  | $↓$ | $1$ | $-6$ | $8$ |
|  | $1$ | $-6$ | $8$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-1}={x}^{2}-6x+8,
$$

which means

$$
p(x)=(x-1)({x}^{2}-6x+8).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-1)(x-2)(x-4).\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-1)$ has an exponent of $1$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=1$ has multiplicity $1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Index of a Term Given the Recursive Formula
questions.problem:
What is the index of the term $192$ for the geometric sequence below?

$$
f(n+1)=2f(n),\,f(1)=3,\,n\ge 1
$$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
This geometric sequence is given as a recurrence relation, i.e.,

$$
f(n+1)=r\cdot f(n).
$$

Therefore:

$$
f(1)=3,\,r=2.
$$

We're interested in finding $n$ such that $f(n)=192.$ Using the formula for the $n$th term, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(n) & =f(1)\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\ 192 & =3\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\ \frac{192}{3} & ={2}^{n-1} \\ 64 & ={2}^{n-1} \\ {2}^{6} & ={2}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the exponents gives:

$$
6=n-1\,⟹\,n=7
$$

Therefore, $192$ is the $7$th term of the sequence.

questions.knowledge_point: Cases Reducing to Solving a Quadratic by Factoring
questions.problem:
Given that $-2{x}^{2}-4kx-8k=0,$ where $k$ is a **positive** constant, has exactly one real solution, what is the value of $k?$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
A quadratic equation has exactly one real root if the discriminant is equal to zero: $D=0.$

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

$$
a=-2,\,b=-4k,\,c=-8k
$$

So, computing the discriminant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={b}^{2}-4ac \\  & =(-4k)^{2}-4(-2)(-8k) \\  & =16{k}^{2}-64k.\end{aligned}
$$

To have exactly one real solution, we need $D=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}16{k}^{2}-64k & =0 \\ 16k(k-4) & =0 \\ k & =0,4\end{aligned}
$$

Since $k$ must be positive, we conclude that $k=4.$

questions.knowledge_point: Estimating a Variance or Standard Deviation
questions.problem:
Consider the frequency table below for a continuous variable $x.$ Assuming that the observations within each class interval are uniformly distributed, the total number of observations is $n=20,$ and the estimated sample mean is $\overset{―}{x}\approx 13.5.$

| Range | Frequency $({f}_{i})$ |
| --- | --- |
| $0\le x<10$ | $8$ |
| $10\le x<20$ | $7$ |
| $20\le x<30$ | $5$ |

$$

$$

Based on these distributional assumptions, find the standard estimate for the sample standard deviation ${\sigma }_{n}.$

Rounded to one decimal place, ${\sigma }_{n}\approx $
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Given a frequency table containing continuous data split into $K$ classes, the variance can be estimated as follows:

$$
{\sigma }_{n}^{2}\approx \frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{K}{f}_{i}\cdot ({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},
$$

where

- ${f}_{i}$ is the frequency of the $i$th class,

- ${m}_{i}$ is the midpoint of the $i$th class,

- $n$ is the total number of observations, and

- $\overset{―}{x}$ is the mean.

To find the variance, we add columns to our table for the midpoints of each interval, the squared deviations of the midpoints from the mean, and the products of the squared deviations and frequencies.

| Range | ${f}_{i}$ | ${m}_{i}$ | ${({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ | ${f}_{i}{({m}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})}^{2}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0\le x<10$ | $8$ | $5$ | $72.25$ | $578$ |
| $10\le x<20$ | $7$ | $15$ | $2.25$ | $15.75$ |
| $20\le x<30$ | $5$ | $25$ | $132.25$ | $661.25$ |

$$

$$

Then, we divide the sum of all the values in the last column by $20$ (the total number of observations):

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n}^{2} & \approx \frac{578+15.75+661.25}{20} \\  & =\frac{1255}{20} \\  & =62.75\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the standard deviation is the square root of the variance:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{n} & =\sqrt{62.75}\approx 7.9\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Similarity Transformations
questions.problem:
Which of the following transformations map any polygon to a similar polygon?

I. - Stretching with a stretch factor of $2$ in the $x$-direction and a stretch factor of $4$ in the $y$-direction
II. - Translation by $3$ units to the left and $4$ units upward
III. - Dilation of scale factor $2$ with center $O,$ then reflection across the $y$-axis
questions.worked_solution:
A similarity transformation is any transformation made up of rigid motions (rotations, reflections, and translations) and dilations.

A similarity transformation will map any polygon to a similar polygon.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the transformations in turn.

- Transformation I includes stretching with different factors in the $x$- and $y$-direction. Thus, it is not a similarity transformation.

- Transformation II is a combination of two translations, which are rigid motions. Thus, it is a similarity transformation.

- Transformation III is a combination of dilation of scale factor $2$ and a reflection. Thus, it is a similarity transformation.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Computing an Inverse Function Using the Definition
questions.problem:
Suppose that $f(x)=2x+6$ and $g(x)=\frac{x}{2}+k.$ If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then $k=$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
If $g$ is the inverse of $f,$ then we must have:

$$
g(f(x))=x
$$

To find $g(f(x)),$ we write down the function $g$ and replace every occurrence of $x$ with $f(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}g(x) & =\frac{x}{2}+k \\ g(f(x)) & =\frac{f(x)}{2}+k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $f(x)=2x+6$ into the right-hand side of our expression and simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(f(x)) & =\frac{f(x)}{2}+k \\  & =\frac{2x+6}{2}+k \\  & =x+3+k\end{aligned}
$$

However, we also know that $g(f(x))=x.$ Equating the expression above with $x$ and solving for $k$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+3+k & =x \\ \cancel{x}+3+k & =\cancel{x} \\ 3+k & =0 \\ k & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Classifying Even and Odd Functions Using the Algebraic Definition
questions.problem: Is the function $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-2x$ even, odd, or neither?
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that

- a function is even if $f(-x)=f(x)$ for all $x$

- a function is odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$ for all $x$

Computing $f(-x)$ for the given function and comparing it to $f(x),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =2(-x)^{3}-2(-x) \\  & =-2{x}^{3}+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)\ne f(x),$ the function is not even.

Lastly, we compute $-f(x)$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}-f(x) & =-(2{x}^{3}-2x) \\  & =-2{x}^{3}+2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f(-x)=-f(x),$ the function is odd.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Index of a Term Given Two Terms
questions.problem:
Given an arithmetic sequence that has ${a}_{4}=13$ and ${a}_{8}=41,$ what is the index of the term $90?$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
To construct the formula for the sequence, we need to know the common difference $d$ and the first term ${a}_{1}.$

Since we are given ${a}_{4}=13$ and ${a}_{8}=41,$ we can find the common difference by dividing the total difference by the number of jumps:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{{a}_{8}-{a}_{4}}{8-4} \\  & =\frac{41-13}{8-4} \\  & =\frac{28}{4} \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since ${a}_{4}=13$ is $3$ jumps after ${a}_{1},$ we can determine the first term of the sequence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{4} & ={a}_{1}+3d \\ 13 & ={a}_{1}+3(7) \\ 13 & ={a}_{1}+21 \\ -8 & ={a}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the formula for the $n$th term is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)d \\  & =-8+(n-1)(7) \\  & =-8+7n-7 \\  & =7n-15\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for the value of $n$ that gives ${a}_{n}=90,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & =7n-15 \\ 90 & =7n-15 \\ 105 & =7n \\ \frac{105}{7} & =n \\ 15 & =n\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $90$ is the $15$th term of the sequence.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Common Ratio Given Some Additional Information About the Geometric Sequence
questions.problem:
The third term of a geometric sequence is $108$ and its fifth term is $3.$  Find the common ratio $r$ of this sequence given that $r$ is positive.

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the common ratio $r$ of a geometric sequence given two terms ${a}_{m}$ and ${a}_{n},$ we use the formula

$$
{r}^{n-m}=\frac{{a}_{n}}{{a}_{m}}.
$$

In this case, we're given ${a}_{5}=3$ and ${a}_{3}=108.$ Substituting $n=5$ and $m=3$ into the formula, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{5-3} & =\frac{{a}_{5}}{{a}_{3}} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{3}{108} \\ {r}^{2} & =\frac{1}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, solving the equation for $r$ and considering that $r$ is positive, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{2} & =\frac{1}{36} \\ {r}^{2} & ={(\frac{1}{6})}^{2} \\ r & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing the Equation of a Parabola With Leading Coefficients in Vertex Form
questions.problem:
The curve $y=4{x}^{2}-24x+24$ can be written as $y=a(x+b)^{2}+c.$ Calculate $a+b+c.$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
To express the equation of the parabola in vertex form, we need to complete the square. 

First, we take out a factor of $4$ from the entire expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-24x+24 & =4({x}^{2}-6x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we complete the square for the expression inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-6x+6 & = \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 3\cdot x+6 & = \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+6 & = \\ ({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3\cdot x+{3}^{2})-{3}^{2}+6 & = \\ (x-3)^{2}-{3}^{2}+6 & = \\ (x-3)^{2}-9+6 & = \\ (x-3)^{2}-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute this result back into our original expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}^{2}-6x+6) & = \\ 4((x-3)^{2}-3) & = \\ 4(x-3)^{2}-12\end{aligned}
$$

So,  $a+b+c=4+(-3)+(-12)=-11.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements About Operations on Polynomials
questions.problem:
If $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ are polynomials of degree $3$ and $7,$ respectively, which of the following statements are true?

I. - $P+Q$ is always a polynomial of degree $10$
II. - $P-Q$ is always a polynomial of degree $4$
III. - $P\cdot Q$ is always a polynomial of degree $10$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's look at each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, suppose $P(x)={x}^{3}$ and $Q(x)={x}^{7}.$ Then $P+Q={x}^{3}+{x}^{7},$ which is not a polynomial of degree $10.$

- Statement II is false. For example, suppose $P(x)={x}^{3}$ and $Q(x)={x}^{7}.$ Then $P-Q={x}^{3}-{x}^{7},$ which is not a polynomial of degree $4.$

- Statement III is true. The highest-degree terms in $P$ and $Q$ must contain ${x}^{3}$ and ${x}^{7},$ respectively. Therefore, the highest-degree term in $P\cdot Q$ must contain ${x}^{3}\cdot {x}^{7}={x}^{3+7}={x}^{10},$ meaning that $P\cdot Q$ has degree $10.$

In conclusion, only statement III is true.

questions.problem:
Given that $f(x)=|x-4|+2,$ on which of the following intervals is $f(x)$ invertible?

I. - $x\in (-\infty ,3)$
II. - $x\in (1,\infty )$
III. - $x\in (-\infty ,5]$
questions.worked_solution:
The graph of the function $f(x)=|x-4|+2$ can be obtained in the following way:

- Take the curve $y=|x|.$

- Translate it by $4$ units to the right,  to get $y=|x-4|.$

- Finally, translate $y=|x-4|$ by $2$ units up to get $f(x)=|x-4|+2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/56956d0f23ae6828098507712fd00525dc4f114a195716dc16e63d8475e9c143.png)

A function is invertible on a particular interval if and only if it's a one-to-one function on that interval. To determine the intervals on which the function is invertible, we use the horizontal line test. 

- The function $f(x)$ is invertible on the interval $x\in (-\infty ,3).$  Indeed, on this interval, any horizontal line will intersect the curve at most once, no matter where we draw the line.

- The function $f(x)$ is not invertible on any of the intervals $x\in (1,\infty )$  and $(-\infty ,5].$ On each of these intervals, some horizontal lines will intersect the curve more than once.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

$$
\begin{aligned}3\sqrt[6]{3x+13}-6 & =0 \\ 3\sqrt[6]{3x+13} & =6 \\ \sqrt[6]{3x+13} & =2 \\ (\sqrt[6]{3x+13})^{6} & ={2}^{6} \\ 3x+13 & =64 \\ 3x & =51 \\ x & =17\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
What is the diameter of a circle if its area is $\frac{9}{25}\pi ?$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of a circle is $A=\pi {r}^{2}$, where $r$ is the radius. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{9}{25}\pi  & =\pi {r}^{2} \\ \frac{9}{25}\cancel{\pi } & =\cancel{\pi }{r}^{2} \\ r & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{25}} \\ r & =\frac{3}{5}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the diameter is

$$
d=2\cdot r=2\cdot \frac{3}{5}=\frac{6}{5}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Maps Presented in Function Notation That Are Rigid Motions
questions.problem:
Which of the following transformations map every polygon to a congruent polygon?

I. - $(x,y)↦(x-1,y)$
II. - $(x,y)↦(-y,x)$
III. - $(x,y)↦(2x,y)$
questions.worked_solution:
A rigid motion is a transformation that preserves distances. There are three types of rigid motions:

- Translations

- Rotations

- Reflections

Also, two polygons are congruent if and only if one can be mapped to another using a combination of rigid motions.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the transformations in turn.

- Transformation I is a translation of $1$ unit to the right. This is a rigid motion. So, it maps every polygon to a congruent polygon.

- Transformation II is a rotation of ${90}^{∘}$ counterclockwise about the origin. This is a rigid motion. So, it maps every polygon to a congruent polygon.

- Transformation III is a stretch with a stretch factor of $2$ in the $x$-direction. This is *not* a rigid motion. So, it does not map every polygon to a congruent polygon.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
Find the root of $f(x)=4{log}_{4}(-3x)+2.$

questions.worked_solution:
To find the root of $f(x)$, we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
4{log}_{4}(-3x)+2=0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{log}_{4}(-3x)+2 & =0 \\ 4{log}_{4}(-3x) & =-2 \\ {log}_{4}(-3x) & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ {4}^{{log}_{4}(-3x)} & ={4}^{-1/2} \\ -3x & =\frac{1}{{4}^{1/2}} \\ -3x & =\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =-\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the root of $f(x)$ is $x=-\frac{1}{6}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Reciprocal Ratio of a Quadrantal Angle
questions.problem:
Find the value of $\operatorname{sec}0+\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
The angles $0$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}$ are quadrantal angles. Let's draw out the quadrantal angles on the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/792a778286533d589a3410223aaf197b07e64ea77566042d7bb8ac13fbad9768.png)

- Let's first consider the angle $0.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $0$ corresponds to the point $(1,0).$  Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}0=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{sec}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sec}0=\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}0}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

- Now, let's consider the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{2}$ corresponds to the point $(0,1).$  Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})=1.$ Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{2})}=\frac{1}{1}=1.
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\operatorname{sec}0+\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{2})=1+1=2.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Multiplicity of a Root of a Cubic Polynomial Using Synthetic Division
questions.problem:
What is the multiplicity of the root $x=4$ in the polynomial $p(x)={x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}+32?$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
Since $x=4$ is a root of $p(x),$ the factor theorem tells us that $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x).$

Because $(x-4)$ is a factor of $p(x),$ we know that $(x-4)$ divides $p(x)$ with no remainder. So, to begin factoring $p(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-4)$ using synthetic division:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $4$ | $1$ | $-6$ | $0$ | $32$ |
|  | $↓$ | $4$ | $-8$ | $-32$ |
|  | $1$ | $-2$ | $-8$ | $0$ |

Therefore,

$$
\frac{p(x)}{x-4}={x}^{2}-2x-8,
$$

which means that

$$
p(x)=(x-4)({x}^{2}-2x-8).
$$

We can factor the quadratic factor even further, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =(x-4)(x+2)(x-4) \\  & =(x+2)(x-4)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The factor $(x-4)$ has an exponent of $2$ in the factored form of $p(x).$ So the root $x=4$ has multiplicity $2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Logarithm Without a Calculator Using the Change of Base Formula
questions.problem:
Calculate ${log}_{8}(32)$ without using a calculator.

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
We use the change of base formula:

$$
{log}_{a}X=\frac{{log}_{b}X}{{log}_{b}a}
$$

In our case, $a=8,$ and $X=32.$ Since both $a$ and $X$ are powers of $2,$ we set $b=2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{8}(32) & =\frac{{log}_{2}(32)}{{log}_{2}(8)} \\  & =\frac{{log}_{2}({2}^{5})}{{log}_{2}({2}^{3})} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The Venn diagram shown above represents two events $A$ and $B$ and the number of outcomes in each region of the sample space.

Given that every outcome is equally likely, find $P({A}^{'}\cup {B}^{'}).$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the probability of an event using a Venn diagram, we count the number of outcomes in the region that represents the event, and divide by the total number of outcomes of the sample space $S.$

In the Venn diagram, ${A}^{'}\cup {B}^{'}$ is represented by the area outside the circle $B$ or outside the circle $A$ (see the illustration below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/6a3bb7b671e45aeb15d3239cae6fcedb7c36e52b15141d66b23e65066ab37edc.png)

We count up the outcomes:

- The number of outcomes in ${A}^{'}\cup {B}^{'}$ is 

$$
2+5+1=8
$$

- The total number of outcomes in $S$ is

$$
2+9+5+1=17.
$$

So, we have

$$
P({A}^{'}\cup {B}^{'})=\frac{8}{17}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining where a Tangent Line Intersects an Axis
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=6\sqrt{x}+5x-13.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6\sqrt{x}+5x-13) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(6{x}^{1/2}+5x) \\  & =3{x}^{-1/2}+5\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{'}(1)=3(1)^{-1/2}+5=8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =8(x-1) \\ y & =8x-8-2 \\ y & =8x-10.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =8x-10 \\ x & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(\frac{5}{4},0).$

questions.knowledge_point: Classifying a Product or Quotient of Numbers
questions.problem:
Which of the following expressions are **irrational**?

I. - ${8}^{5}\cdot \sqrt{36}$
II. - ${3}^{20}\cdot 7.0523$
III. - $\sqrt{2}\cdot {2}^{-15}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that: 

- the product of two rational numbers is *always* rational:

$$
\text{rational}\times \text{rational}=\text{rational}
$$

- the product of a nonzero rational number and an irrational number is *always* irrational:

$$
\text{rational}\times \text{irrational}=\text{irrational}
$$

- the product of two irrational numbers is *sometimes* rational and *sometimes* irrational.

With that in mind, let's examine the statements.

- Expression I is rational. Notice that $\sqrt{36}=6$ is a rational number. The number ${8}^{5}$ is rational too. So, their product must be rational.

- Expression II is rational. Since both ${3}^{20}$ and $7.0523$ are rational, their product must be rational.

- Expression III is irrational. Since $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational and ${2}^{-15}$ is rational, their product must be irrational.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Lowest Common Denominator of Two Fractions
questions.problem:
Find the lowest common denominator of $\frac{5}{20}$ and $\frac{7}{45}.$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the lowest common denominator of two fractions, we first find the prime factorization of both denominators.

- We start by finding the prime factorization of $20:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/7e03a139fc3afa7df4d7f32ecf42f8f30d19bfe0415725f47fe5be63301899b5.png)

Therefore, $20={2}^{2}\cdot 5.$

- Next, we find the prime factorization of $45:$

Therefore, $45={3}^{2}\cdot 5.$

So, we have the following prime factorizations:

$$
\begin{aligned}20 & ={2}^{2}\cdot 5 \\ 45 & ={3}^{2}\cdot 5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we write down every prime factor that is shown above, and we raise each prime factor to the highest power given in either factorization:

- the highest power of $2$ is $2$

- the highest power of $3$ is $2$

- the highest power of $5$ is $1$

Therefore, the lowest common denominator is ${2}^{2}\cdot {3}^{2}\cdot 5=180.$

questions.problem:
In a zoo, there are $12$ camels. If the ratio of camels to monkeys is $3:7,$ how many monkeys are there in the zoo?

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
We start with the ratio $3:7$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{3}{7}
$$

In this fraction, the numerator represents the number of camels and the denominator represents the number of monkeys.

We can make a numerator of $12$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $4$:

$$
\frac{3\times 4}{7\times 4}=\frac{12}{28}
$$

Therefore, there are $28$ monkeys in the zoo.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at a Particular Moment
questions.problem:
The displacement $s$ (in meters) relative to a fixed origin $O$ of a particle moving in a straight line along the $x$-axis is given by the equation $s(t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}(t+1)+6}{{t}^{2}+1}$, where $t$ is the time, measured in seconds. Find the position ${s}_{0}$ and velocity ${v}_{0}$ of the particle at the initial moment of time $t=0\,\text{s}.$

${s}_{0}=$
{{field-1}}$\text{m}\,\text{and}\,$
${v}_{0}=$
{{field-2}}$\text{m/s}$
questions.worked_solution:
To calculate the initial position, we substitute $t=0$ it into the equation $s(t)=\frac{\operatorname{ln}(t+1)+6}{{t}^{2}+1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{0} & =s(0) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}(0+1)+6}{{0}^{2}+1} \\  & =6\,\text{m}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}(t+1)+6}{{t}^{2}+1}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{t+1}\cdot ({t}^{2}+1)-(\operatorname{ln}(t+1)+6)\cdot 2t}{({t}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{t}^{2}+1-2t(t+1)(\operatorname{ln}(t+1)+6)}{(t+1)({t}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the velocity at $t=0\,\text{s},$ we substitute $t=0$ into the velocity function above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{0} & =v(0) \\  & =\frac{{0}^{2}+1-2(0)(0+1)(\operatorname{ln}(0+1)+6)}{(0+1)({0}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot {1}^{2}} \\  & =1\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding Left- and Right-Continuity
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/history-question-import-2026-10-04/import-ready/assets/3bb1c35edab6cecb8bdc0021b7d931c4a8284d02385c0d2398e0b3ca4fb473c0.png)

Which of the following statements are true regarding the function $f(x)$ plotted above?

II. - The function is right-continuous at $x=0$
III. - The function is continuous at $x=0$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. The function is left-continuous at $x=0,$ since the left-sided limit is equal to the function value:

$$
{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x)=0=f(0)
$$

- Statement II is false. The function is not right-continuous at $x=0,$ since the right-sided limit is not equal to the function value:

$$
{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x)=1\ne 0=f(0)
$$

- Statement III is false. In order for the function to be continuous at $x=0,$ it must be both left-continuous and right-continuous. However, we have already determined that the function is not right-continuous at this point.

In conclusion, only statement I is true.

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{\pi }{6}$ corresponds to the point $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}(\frac{\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}(\frac{\pi }{6})}=\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=2.
$$

Finally, evaluating $v(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{6}$ we have

$$
4{csc}^{2}(\frac{\pi }{6})=4{(2)}^{2}=16.
$$

questions.problem:
The position $s(t)$ of a particle at time $t$ is given by 

$$
s(t)=5{e}^{t}+2\operatorname{ln}t+{t}^{2},\,t>0.
$$

Calculate the velocity at time $t=2.$ Round your answer to the nearest integer.

questions.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the velocity function by differentiating the position function:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5{e}^{t}+2\operatorname{ln}t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =5{e}^{t}+\frac{2}{t}+2t\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the velocity at $t=2,$ we substitute $t=2$ into the velocity function above:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =5{e}^{2}+\frac{2}{2}+2(2) \\  & =5{e}^{2}+5 \\  & =41.945… \\  & \approx 42\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.problem:
Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to 25}\frac{x-25}{\sqrt{x}-5}.$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=25$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 25}\frac{x-25}{\sqrt{x}-5} & =\frac{25-25}{\sqrt{25}-5}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 25}\frac{x-25}{\sqrt{x}-5} & ={lim}_{x\to 25}\frac{(x-25)(\sqrt{x}+5)}{(\sqrt{x}-5)(\sqrt{x}+5)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 25}\frac{(x-25)(\sqrt{x}+5)}{{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}-{5}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 25}\frac{(x-25)(\sqrt{x}+5)}{x-25} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 25}(\sqrt{x}+5) \\  & =\sqrt{25}+5 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
${lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt{4x-3}-3}{x-3}=$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt{4x-3}-3}{x-3} & =\frac{\sqrt{4(3)-3}-3}{3-3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{9}-3}{3-3} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt{4x-3}-3}{x-3} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(\sqrt{4x-3}-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)}{(x-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(\sqrt{4x-3})^{2}-{3}^{2}}{(x-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{4x-3-9}{(x-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{4x-12}{(x-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{4(x-3)}{(x-3)(\sqrt{4x-3}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{4}{\sqrt{4x-3}+3} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{4(3)-3}+3} \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{9}+3} \\  & =\frac{4}{6} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Simplify the expression $\operatorname{tan}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{csc}\theta .$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the identities $\operatorname{tan}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta }$ and $\operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta },$ and we substitute them into the given expression:

$$
\operatorname{tan}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{csc}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta }
$$

Now, we multiply the three quantities:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta } \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}\theta }}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta }} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{tan}\theta \operatorname{cos}\theta \operatorname{csc}\theta =1.$

questions.problem:
Given that  $7\operatorname{sin}\theta =17\operatorname{cos}\theta ,$ calculate $\operatorname{tan}\theta .$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the identity $\operatorname{tan}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta }.$

To write the equation in terms of $\operatorname{tan}\theta $ only, we divide both sides of the equation by $\operatorname{cos}\theta ,$ and apply the above identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}7\operatorname{sin}\theta  & =17\operatorname{cos}\theta  \\ 7\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta } & =17\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta } \\ 7\operatorname{tan}\theta  & =17\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we isolate $\operatorname{tan}\theta $ by dividing both sides of the equation by $7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7\operatorname{tan}\theta }{7} & =\frac{17}{7} \\ \operatorname{tan}\theta  & =\frac{17}{7}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Simplify the trigonometric expression $\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sec}\theta \operatorname{cot}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}.$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's interpret the fraction as a division:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sec}\theta \operatorname{cot}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}=(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sec}\theta \operatorname{cot}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta )÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1)
$$

Then, we recall the identities $\operatorname{cot}\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }$ and $\operatorname{sec}\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta },$ and we substitute them into the above expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sec}\theta \operatorname{cot}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta )÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1) & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta )÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we simplify, turn the division into multiplication, and then simplify again:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta }{\operatorname{sin}\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta )÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1) & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}\theta })÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \cancel{\operatorname{sin}\theta }}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}\theta }\cdot \cancel{\operatorname{sin}\theta }})÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1)÷(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1) \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}\theta -1)\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{\operatorname{cos}\theta -\operatorname{sec}\theta \operatorname{cot}\theta \operatorname{sin}\theta }{\operatorname{cos}\theta -1}=1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of an Inverse Function
questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=x+\operatorname{cos}x$ and the point $P(0,1)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$  calculate ${({f}^{-1})}^{'}(1).$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =x+\operatorname{cos}x \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =1-\operatorname{sin}x \\ {f}^{'}(0) & =1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(0,1)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(1,0)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

| **$x$** | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{'}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $4$ | $-9$ | $0$ |
| $5$ | $3$ | $-2$ |

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{'}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Substituting $x=3,$ we have

$$
({f}^{-1})^{'}(3)=\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(3))}.
$$

From the table, we obtain ${f}^{-1}(3)=5$ and ${f}^{'}(5)=-2.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{'}(3) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(3))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}(5)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-2)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem:
The number of computers affected by the spread of some ransomware after $t$ days can be modeled by the function $f(t)=\frac{100\,({t}^{3}+2)}{t+1}.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change in the number of infected computers when $t=9$ days?

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change in the spread when $t=9$ days is equal to ${f}^{'}(9).$ 

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{100\,({t}^{3}+2)}{t+1}) \\  & =\frac{100(3{t}^{2})(t+1)-100({t}^{3}+2)(1)}{{(t+1)}^{2}} \\  & =100\cdot \frac{2{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}-2}{{(t+1)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(9) & =100\cdot \frac{2(9)^{3}+3(9)^{2}-2}{{((9)+1)}^{2}} \\  & =100\cdot \frac{1\,458+243-2}{100} \\  & =1\,699.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change in the spread when $t=9$ is $1\,699$ computers per day.

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Right Riemann Sum in Sigma Notation
questions.problem:
Write the expression for the Riemann sum from part 7 in sigma notation.

The right Riemann sum $\,=\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}0.5(i-$
{{field-1}} ${i}^{2})$
questions.worked_solution:
The right Riemann sum for $y=f(x)$ with a regular step size in sigma notation is

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$ 

In our case, we have $n=4$ subintervals, $a=0,$ $b=2,$ and $Δx=0.5.$

Therefore, using sigma notation, the right Riemann sum can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})Δx & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f(a+iΔx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}f(0+i\cdot 0.5)\cdot 0.5 \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}0.5f(0.5i) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}0.5(2(0.5i)-{(0.5i)}^{2}) \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{4}0.5(i-0.25{i}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
questions.problem:
Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to {5}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{2x-1}-3}{x-5}.$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {5}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{2x-1}-3}{x-5} & =\frac{\sqrt{2(5)-1}-3}{5-5}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {5}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{2x-1}-3}{x-5} & ={lim}_{x\to {5}^{+}}\frac{(\sqrt{2x-1}-3)(\sqrt{2x-1}+3)}{(x-5)(\sqrt{2x-1}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {5}^{+}}\frac{{(\sqrt{2x-1})}^{2}-{3}^{2}}{(x-5)(\sqrt{2x-1}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {5}^{+}}\frac{2x-1-9}{(x-5)(\sqrt{2x-1}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {5}^{+}}\frac{2x-10}{(x-5)(\sqrt{2x-1}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {5}^{+}}\frac{2(x-5)}{(x-5)(\sqrt{2x-1}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {5}^{+}}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2x-1}+3} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{2(5)-1}+3} \\  & =\frac{2}{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining Whether a Function is Left- or Right-Continuous From a Graph
questions.worked_solution:
To determine whether $f(x)$ is right-continuous at $x=c,$ we need to check whether the right-sided limit is equal to the function value.

The function has three discontinuities: $x=-2$, $x=0$ and $x=2.$

- At $x=-2$  the function is neither left- nor right-continuous because it's undefined at this point.

- At $x=0$ the function is not right-continuous because

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x)=0\ne -1=f(0).
$$

- At $x=2$ the function is right-continuous because

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{2}^{+}}f(x)=-2=f(2).
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $x=2$ only.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining an Intercept of a Tangent or Normal Line to a Curve Given in Implicit Form
questions.worked_solution:
First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(3,\,3).$  Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{'},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(9) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ 6x-4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ -4y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-6x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{-6x}{-4y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{3x}{2y}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at the point $(3,\,3)$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & ={(\frac{3x}{2y})}_{(3,\,3)} \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 3}{2\cdot 3} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line is ${m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3/2}=-\frac{2}{3}.$ We can write the equation of the normal at the point $(3,\,3)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-{y}_{1}) & ={m}^{'}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ (y-3) & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-3) \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-3)+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we just need to find where this normal line intersects the $y$-axis. At the point $P$ the $x$-coordinate is $0,$ so we set $x=0$ and solve for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-3)+3 \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}(0-3)+3 \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}(-3)+3 \\ y & =2+3 \\ y & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of $P$ are $(0,\,5).$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}+1)+3x$ and the point $P(0,0)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$  calculate ${({f}^{-1})}^{'}(0).$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(0,0).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{ln}({x}^{2}+1)+3x \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+1}+3 \\ {f}^{'}(0) & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(0,0)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(0,0)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}(0)} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Since $(3,3)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(3,3)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Derivative Using Properties of Inverse Functions
questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=\frac{3x+1}{2x-1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(2).$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ For $x\ne \frac{1}{2},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1} & =2 \\ \frac{3x+1}{2x-1}\cdot (2x-1) & =2\cdot (2x-1) \\ \frac{3x+1}{\cancel{(2x-1)}}\cdot \cancel{(2x-1)} & =4x-2 \\ 3x+1 & =4x-2 \\ 1+2 & =4x-3x \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=3.$

Now we calculate ${f}^{'}(3),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3x+1}{2x-1} \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =-\frac{5}{(2x-1)^{2}} \\ {f}^{'}(3) & =-\frac{5}{{(2\cdot 3-1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{5}{{(5)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x)=3x+\sqrt{x}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(2).$

questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{'}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ 3x+\sqrt{x} & =2 \\ \sqrt{x} & =2-3x \\ x & =4-12x+9{x}^{2} \\ 9{x}^{2}-13x+4 & =0 \\ (9x-4)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =\frac{4}{9},\,1.\end{aligned}
$$

Checking the solutions, we notice that only $x=\frac{4}{9}$ satisfies the equation $3x+\sqrt{x}=2.$ Therefore, we discard $x=1$ and conclude that ${f}^{-1}(2)=\frac{4}{9}.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{'}(\frac{4}{9}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =3x+\sqrt{x} \\ {f}^{'}(x) & =3+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ {f}^{'}(\frac{4}{9}) & =3+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{(\frac{4}{9})}} \\ {f}^{'}(\frac{4}{9}) & =3+\frac{3}{4} \\ {f}^{'}(\frac{4}{9}) & =\frac{15}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{'}(1) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}({f}^{-1}(1))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{'}(\frac{4}{9})} \\  & =\frac{4}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.problem:
${lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4\sqrt{x+4}-x-8}{{x}^{2}}=$

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4\sqrt{x+4}-x-8}{{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[4\sqrt{x+4}-x-8]}^{'}}{[{x}^{2}]^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+4}}-1]}{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{4\sqrt{x+4}-x-8}{{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+4}}-1]}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[\frac{2}{\sqrt{x+4}}-1]}^{'}}{[2x]^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[-\frac{1}{(x+4)\sqrt{x+4}}]}{2} \\  & =\frac{[-\frac{1}{(0+4)\sqrt{0+4}}]}{2} \\  & =\frac{[-\frac{1}{4(2)}]}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:

If we plug in $x=3$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-6x+9}{8\sqrt{x+1}-2x-10} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{[{x}^{2}-6x+9]}^{'}}{[8\sqrt{x+1}-2x-10]^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{2x-6}{\frac{4}{\sqrt{x+1}}-2} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{2(x+1)^{-1/2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-6x+9}{8\sqrt{x+1}-2x-10} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{2(x+1)^{-1/2}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{[x-3]}^{'}}{[2(x+1)^{-1/2}-1]^{'}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{1}{-(x+1)^{-3/2}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to 3}(x+1)^{3/2} \\  & =-(3+1)^{3/2} \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem:
Research of a factory assembly line shows that the number of units $f$ produced in $x$ hours can be modeled by the function $f(x)={x}^{2}+20x.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of production when $x=2$ hours?

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of production when $x=2$ hours is equal to ${f}^{'}(2).$

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+20x) \\  & =2x+20.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(2) & =2(2)+20 \\  & =4+20 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of production when $x=2$ hours is $24$ units per hour.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Intercepts of a Normal Line
questions.problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt[4]{x}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $).$
questions.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt[4]{x}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt[4]{{x}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{'}(1)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt[4]{{1}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=-2.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-2\cdot (x-1) \\ y & =-2x+2+2 \\ y & =-2x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+4 & =0 \\ 2x & =4 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(\,2,0\,).$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Root Rule to Compute a Limit
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the quotient rule, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to -1}\frac{2x+8}{\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{4}+5}}=\frac{{lim}_{x\to -1}(2x+8)}{{lim}_{x\to -1}\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{4}+5}}\,.
$$

We calculate the limits of the numerator and the denominator separately.

For the numerator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}(2x+8) & =2{lim}_{x\to -1}x+{lim}_{x\to -1}8 \\  & =2(-1)+8 \\  & =6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the root rule in the denominator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}\sqrt[3]{3{x}^{4}+5} & =\sqrt[3]{{lim}_{x\to -1}(3{x}^{4}+5)} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{3(-1)^{4}+5} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{8} \\  & =2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{\sqrt{x-1}-2}{x-5} & =\frac{\sqrt{5-1}-2}{5-5}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{\sqrt{x-1}-2}{x-5} & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{(\sqrt{x-1}-2)(\sqrt{x-1}+2)}{(x-5)(\sqrt{x-1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{{(\sqrt{x-1})}^{2}-{2}^{2}}{(x-5)(\sqrt{x-1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{x-1-4}{(x-5)(\sqrt{x-1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{x-5}{(x-5)(\sqrt{x-1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-1}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5-1}+2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{5x+6}-4}{x-2} & =\frac{\sqrt{5(2)+6}-4}{2-2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{16}-4}{2-2} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{\sqrt{5x+6}-4}{x-2} & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(\sqrt{5x+6}-4)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)}{(x-2)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{(\sqrt{5x+6})^{2}-{4}^{2}}{(x-2)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{5x+6-16}{(x-2)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{5x-10}{(x-2)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{5(x-2)}{(x-2)(\sqrt{5x+6}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{5}{\sqrt{5x+6}+4} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{5(2)+6}+4} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{16}+4} \\  & =\frac{5}{4+4} \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{x-8}{4-\sqrt{2x}} & ={lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{(x-8)(4+\sqrt{2x})}{(4-\sqrt{2x})(4+\sqrt{2x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{(x-8)(4+\sqrt{2x})}{{4}^{2}-{(\sqrt{2x})}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{(x-8)(4+\sqrt{2x})}{16-2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{(x-8)(4+\sqrt{2x})}{-2(x-8)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{4+\sqrt{2x}}{-2} \\  & =\frac{4+\sqrt{2(8)}}{-2} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:

Answer: {{answer}}
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=2$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{x-2}{2x-\sqrt{8x}} & =\frac{2-2}{2(2)-\sqrt{8(2)}}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{x-2}{2x-\sqrt{8x}} & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{(x-2)(2x+\sqrt{8x})}{(2x-\sqrt{8x})(2x+\sqrt{8x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{(x-2)(2x+\sqrt{8x})}{(2x)^{2}-{(\sqrt{8x})}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{(x-2)(2x+\sqrt{8x})}{4{x}^{2}-8x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{(x-2)(2x+\sqrt{8x})}{4x(x-2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}\frac{2x+\sqrt{8x}}{4x} \\  & =\frac{2(2)+\sqrt{8(2)}}{4(2)} \\  & =\frac{4+4}{8} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem:
The function $E(v)=\frac{6v+18}{v+2}$ models the price of electricity, in dollars, based on the number of customers $v$ (in thousands) served the previous month. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the price of electricity when $v=4$ thousand customers?

The instantaneous rate of change when $v=4$ is
{{field-1}} dollars per thousand customers.
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the price when $v=4$ thousand customers is equal to ${E}^{'}(4).$

Now, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{'}(v) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(\frac{6v+18}{v+2}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(6v+18)\cdot (v+2)-(6v+18)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}v}(v+2)}{(v+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(6)\cdot (v+2)-(6v+18)\cdot (1)}{(v+2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6v+12-6v-18}{(v+2)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{6}{(v+2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $v=4,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{'}(4) & =-\frac{6}{((4)+2)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{6}{36} \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the price when $v=4$ thousand customers is $-\frac{1}{6}$ dollars per thousand customers.

$$

questions.problem:
The surface area $A$ of a cube is increasing. Find the instantaneous rate at which the surface area of the cube is changing with respect to its side length at the moment when the side length of the cube is equal to $3\,\text{in}.$

The instantaneous rate of change at the moment when its side length is $3$ inches is equal to
{{field-1}} ${\text{in}}^{2}/\text{in}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We know that the surface area of a cube with side length $s$ is given by 

$$
A=A(s)=6{s}^{2}.
$$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $A(s)$ with respect to $s$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{'}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(6{s}^{2}) \\  & =6(2s) \\  & =12s,\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $s=3$ gives

$$
{A}^{'}(3)=12(3)=36.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the surface area of the cube is changing when its side length is $3\,\text{in}$, is $36$ ${\text{in}}^{2}/\text{in}.$

questions.worked_solution:
We have to solve $h(x)=5,$ or equivalently, $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}+3=5.$

First, we isolate the term $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}$ by subtracting $3$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}+3 & =5 \\ \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we isolate the square root by multiplying by $\frac{3}{2}$ on both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x} & =2 \\ \sqrt{x} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the square root is isolated, we can proceed as usual. Squaring both sides of the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{x} & =3 \\ (\sqrt{x})^{2} & ={3}^{2} \\ x & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check the result by plugging it into the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{9}+3 & \overset{?}{=}5 \\ \frac{2}{3}\cdot 3+3 & \overset{?}{=}5 \\ 2+3 & =5\,\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

The value $x=9$ satisfies the original equation, so we can accept it as a solution.

Therefore, the solution to $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{x}+3=5$  is $x=9.$

First of all, we need to find the slope of the normal line at the point $(4,4).$ Remember that the slope of the normal line, ${m}^{'},$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we will calculate the derivative using implicit differentiation, assuming that $y=y(x).$

$$
\begin{aligned}8y & ={x}^{2}+4x \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+4x) \\ 8\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x+4 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x+4}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{x+2}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & ={(\frac{x+2}{4})|}_{(4,\,4)} \\  & =\frac{4+2}{4} \\  & =\frac{6}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & ={m}^{'}(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-4) \\ y-4 & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{8}{3} \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{20}{3}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{20}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}x & =\frac{20}{3} \\ x & =10\end{aligned}
